newsitem.title: CHINA: Father demands medical parole for China dissident.
newsitem.headline: Father demands medical parole for China dissident.

text.p: The father of a detained Chinese dissident who attempted suicide last year has accused authorities of denying his son medical treatment, a human rights group said on Monday.

Chen Jinyun has demanded that authorities in the eastern city of Hangzhou grant medical parole to his son Chen Longde, the Hong Kong-based Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said.

The dissident attempted suicide in August last year by jumping from a third-floor window because he could not stand beatings inflicted by a labour camp official, his family has said. The labour camp has denied any wrongdoing.
"He has not fully recovered, but they sent him back (to the labour camp)," the human rights centre quoted Chen's father as saying.
"He is still using crutches but they forced him to engage in manual labour," he said. "They want to cripple him for life."
Chen Longde broke his right leg and smashed three teeth and was taken to hospital after his fall, but was sent back to the labour camp last December.

The 39-year-old dissident was detained in May 1996 and ordered to serve three years of re-education through labour for "endangering national security" by sending a petition to parliament demanding the release of political prisoners.
Re-education through labour is an administrative punishment that allows police to incarcerate people suspected of committing petty crimes for up to three years without benefit of trial.
Chen Longde was previously jailed for three years for his role in student-led demonstrations for democracy crushed by the army in Beijing on June 4, 1989, with heavy loss of life.

The official Legal Daily on Sunday dismissed calls for the abolition of re-education through labour, which international human rights groups say has been increasingly used by Beijing to remove dissidents from circulation.

The newspaper defended the 40-year-old system, saying it was needed to maintain social peace and prevent and reduce crime and that it gave people suspected of committing petty crimes a chance to turn over a new leaf.

International human rights groups and Western governments have criticised Beijing for a crackdown on dissent in 1996 that saw almost the entire Chinese pro-democracy movement jailed, intimidated into silence or driven into exile.

China rejects international criticisms of its policies on dissent as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that the right to the bare necessities of life is more important than political rights.
